question: How close to the file-size limit counts as 'near the limit'?
details: Only files that are really about to hit the limit show up, so the list stays short, but there is less warning time before the hard limit.
Warnings come earlier, but many more files get listed and the list gets noisier.
Each repository can tune the threshold, at the cost of one more setting to understand.

question: When the working tree has new debt, should rewriting the baseline refuse, or accept the new items?
options: Refuse unless an explicit override is given
details: An agent cannot get around the ratchet just by rewriting the baseline, but a person who really wants to accept new debt has to pass an extra flag.
Rewriting is simpler, but an agent can erase the ratchet by rewriting the baseline with its new debt included.

question: If an existing item only moves to a different line number (because code was added above it), is it a new item?
options: No, a moved item with the same content is not new
Yes, any file:line not in the baseline is new
details: Ordinary edits near old TODOs don't cause false blocks, but an item counts as the same one by content, not by its exact line.
The rule is simplest, but almost any edit above an existing TODO or duplicate block causes a false block.

question: What should the Stop hook do when there is no baseline file yet?
options: Don't block; suggest creating a baseline
Treat every current item as new and block once
details: Installing the harness causes no surprise block, but the ratchet does nothing until someone creates a baseline.
The ratchet starts working right away, but the first stop in every existing repository blocks on all old debt at once.
The ratchet starts with no user step, but a baseline file appears that nobody chose to create or commit.

question: What counts as 'not noticeably slower' for the Stop hook?
options: At most 1 second added on a typical repository
Only changed files are checked, with no fixed time limit
details: Stopping stays snappy, but the debt check has to stay very light.
Allows more thorough duplicate detection, but every stop has a delay you can feel.
Cost grows with the size of the change rather than the repository, but there is no stated number to test against.

question: How should 'largest item' be measured for the weekly cleanup order?
options: Duplicates first, then near-limit files, then TODOs
details: One order across all kinds that is easy to understand, but a big near-limit file can outrank a duplication problem that is worse.
Duplicated code always gets cleaned first, but small duplicates can come ahead of very large files.
